title:
Comment of Monica Parker in Docket(s)/Project(s) P-15423-000
Submission Date: 10/28/2026

documents.name: 151920.txt
documents.text:
Monica Parker, Anchorage, AK.
As an Alaskan, I strongly oppose DeepGreen’s proposal to install an underwater data center in Cook Inlet. I am deeply concerned about the risks to our marine ecosystem, endangered Cook Inlet beluga whales, salmon fisheries, and the communities that depend on these waters. Equally troubling is the apparent lack of adequate planning to address the project's significant engineering, environmental, and operational challenges.
I understand that data centers are increasingly necessary to support the technology we depend on. However, that does not mean every location or method of powering them is appropriate. Cook Inlet is an extraordinarily dynamic and ecologically important waterway, not a place for a massive, unproven infrastructure experiment. Alaskans should not bear the environmental risks of an outside company's business venture without compelling evidence that the project can be operated safely and responsibly.
ENGINEERING AND OPERATIONAL RISKS
The proposed installation would be located in the deepest channel of the Cook Inlet Forelands, a natural bottleneck characterized by powerful currents, enormous tidal fluctuations, suspended glacial silt, volcanic ash, shifting sand, and frequent seismic activity. These conditions could subject underwater infrastructure to relentless abrasion, sediment exposure, biological growth, and earthquake-related damage.
The proposal includes 66 server hives and more than 300 tidal turbine generators. That is an enormous amount of equipment to install, operate, and maintain in a harsh marine environment. Components will eventually require inspection, repair, and replacement. How will damaged equipment be accessed and repaired? How frequently will maintenance be needed? What happens when critical components fail? What are the plans and costs for decommissioning the infrastructure at the end of its useful life?
These are fundamental questions of feasibility, reliability, and cost. Before this project advances, DeepGreen should be required to demonstrate through independent engineering assessments that its infrastructure can withstand actual Cook Inlet conditions over the long term.
ENDANGERED COOK INLET BELUGA WHALES
Cook Inlet is home to an endangered population of beluga whales that depends on sound to communicate, navigate, locate prey, and respond to its surroundings. NOAA has identified noise as a significant threat to Cook Inlet beluga recovery. The Forelands is also a critical passage between seasonal feeding and calving areas.
An underwater data center and hundreds of tidal generators could introduce new sources of underwater noise. Construction, operation, maintenance, and equipment failure all need to be considered. How loud will the system be? How far will the sound travel? Could it interfere with beluga communication, feeding, movement, or access to critical habitat?
I am particularly concerned about the cumulative effects of placing so much infrastructure in a natural bottleneck that belugas must navigate. A persistent acoustic disturbance could have consequences well beyond the immediate installation site. These risks must be independently evaluated using credible scientific evidence before the project proceeds. Renewable energy is not automatically environmentally harmless.
SALMON, FISHERIES, AND WATER QUALITY
Cook Inlet's fisheries are central to Alaska's economy, food security, traditions, and way of life. We should not gamble with these resources for the speculative benefits of an experimental technology project.
Salmon migrating to streams north of Nikiski must pass through the Forelands. The proposed installation would place extensive infrastructure directly in this important migration corridor, with setnet sites located within three miles of the proposed data center.
Potential impacts extend beyond the physical footprint of the installation. I am concerned about underwater noise, construction and maintenance activities, changes in water temperature, and the possible release of metals or other contaminants. Copper, for example, can be toxic to aquatic organisms at sufficient concentrations. DeepGreen must disclose what materials and coatings its system will use and demonstrate that corrosion, leaks, and accidental releases will not expose salmon or other marine life to harmful contaminants.
I am also concerned about the waste heat generated by a data center reportedly requiring approximately 100 megawatts of power. How will that heat be discharged or dissipated? What will happen during slack tide, when water movement is reduced? What modeling has been conducted to assess localized temperature changes and their effects on salmon and the broader aquatic ecosystem?
The company must also disclose the coolants, coatings, and other substances its system would use, including whether PFAS-containing materials or other persistent chemicals are involved. Any potential release into Cook Inlet must be evaluated. The possibility of contaminating these waters should not be dismissed simply because a release is considered unlikely.
ELECTRICITY DEMAND AND BACKUP POWER
DeepGreen proposes to use more than 300 tidal turbine generators to support the data center's substantial electricity demand. The scale of this proposal raises serious questions about whether its power-generation assumptions are realistic and whether the project can operate reliably under actual tidal conditions.
What happens when tidal generation cannot meet demand? What backup power sources will be used, and what are their environmental impacts? How will the system operate during equipment outages or extended periods of reduced generation?
A data center requiring approximately 100 megawatts could place a substantial burden on the regional electrical system serving the Kenai Peninsula. If supplemental electricity must come from the grid, what upgrades would be required, who would pay for them, and how could the project affect existing ratepayers? 
Homer Electric Association, Alaska Power Association, and other relevant utilities should have a meaningful opportunity to evaluate the project's electrical requirements and potential effects on the regional grid. Alaskans should not discover after the fact that this project requires costly infrastructure upgrades or backup power arrangements that were never adequately considered.
Ocean Renewable Power Company has also been developing tidal energy technology for Alaskan conditions. The scale of DeepGreen's proposal makes it especially important to establish whether its generation capacity, reliability, and environmental assumptions are supported by evidence. A project involving hundreds of generators should not be allowed to proceed without rigorous assessment of its cumulative impacts.
UNPROVEN TECHNOLOGY AND ACCOUNTABILITY
Microsoft's underwater data center experiment demonstrated that the technology could be tested, but it does not establish that a much larger installation would be safe, economical, or environmentally appropriate in Cook Inlet. The experience of a smaller experimental system cannot simply be extrapolated to a proposal involving dozens of server hives and hundreds of tidal generators in one of Alaska's most challenging marine environments.
The question is not merely whether an underwater data center can be built. It is whether this particular project can be operated reliably, maintained economically, and eventually decommissioned without unacceptable environmental harm.
The burden should be on DeepGreen to demonstrate that its proposal is technically feasible, economically viable, and environmentally responsible. Company assurances are not an adequate substitute for transparent technical information, independent scientific review, and enforceable environmental protections.
MY REQUEST TO FERC
I urge FERC to require comprehensive, independent assessments of engineering feasibility, underwater noise, impacts on belugas and salmon migration, water quality, thermal discharge, potential chemical releases, electricity demand, backup power, maintenance, and decommissioning. These assessments must consider the cumulative effects of the entire installation, not evaluate individual components in isolation.
The public must have access to the underlying technical information and a meaningful opportunity to comment before irreversible decisions are made. If DeepGreen cannot demonstrate that it can prevent unacceptable environmental harm and manage the project's substantial operational risks, FERC should deny the application.
Cook Inlet is not an expendable testing ground for an outside company's business venture. Its wildlife, fisheries, and waters sustain Alaskan communities and are part of our heritage. We have a responsibility to protect these resources for future generations, not gamble them on a massive industrial experiment whose long-term consequences remain uncertain.
I strongly oppose DeepGreen's proposed underwater data center in Cook Inlet and urge FERC not to allow this project to proceed without compelling, independently verified evidence that it can operate without unacceptable harm to Alaska's environment, wildlife, fisheries, and communities.
